Count the snowy clues you see.
Read the words to follow the trail.
story: Follow a scent trail through cold Arctic darkness.
Count each group of snowy clues and read the words without wasting the shark's energy.

mission.completion: Slow and steady! The Greenland shark followed the Arctic scent trail.

earlyReader: Which water does it like?
story: Which habitat suits a Greenland shark?

questions.success: Yes! Greenland sharks live in cold Arctic water.
questions.retry: Choose the icy ocean.

earlyReader: How does it usually swim?
story: Which movement saves energy in cold water?

questions.success: Right! It swims slowly and steadily.
questions.retry: Look for the movement that saves energy.

earlyReader: What is a scavenger?
story: Which food might a scavenger eat?

questions.success: Exactly! A scavenger eats animals it finds already dead.
questions.retry: Choose food the shark can find in the sea.

sharks.bookFact: This slow-growing Arctic shark may live for several hundred years.

sharks.name: Shortfin Mako
sharks.imageAuthor: Mark Conlin, SWFSC Large Pelagics Program

decodable: It runs and runs. It has pep!
earlyReader: This is a shortfin mako.
It is the fastest shark in the sea.
Its smooth body cuts through the water.
story: The shortfin mako is the fastest shark in the ocean.
Its pointed snout and smooth, streamlined body help it race after speedy fish.

decodable: It did not sit in a den. It runs on and on.
earlyReader: Makos live far from shore.
They swim in the wide open ocean.
They like warm and cool water.
story: Shortfin makos roam the open ocean in warm and temperate seas around the world.
They travel long distances and rarely rest near the seafloor.

decodable: It ran and ran. It got him!
earlyReader: Makos eat fast fish.
Tuna and mackerel are food.
Squid can be food too.
story: Speedy fish such as tuna and mackerel are favorite mako prey.
A mako must swim even faster than its food to catch a meal.

decodable: It is big, not fat. It is fit to run.
earlyReader: A mako is longer than a couch.
Its snout is pointed like a cone.
Its tail looks like a crescent moon.
story: A grown shortfin mako is often about ten feet long.
Its cone-shaped snout and crescent tail are built for speed.

decodable: A cod hid, but it got the hum.
earlyReader: A mako has big dark eyes.
Its eyes help it spot quick fish.
It also feels moving water on its skin.
story: Large dark eyes help a mako follow fast prey through open water.
Like other sharks, it also senses movement and tiny electric signals nearby.

decodable: Run, run, hop! It can hop up to the sun.
earlyReader: A mako keeps its muscles warm.
Warm muscles help it swim very fast.
It can even leap high out of the sea.
story: A mako keeps its swimming muscles warmer than the water around it.
That warmth powers bursts of great speed and spectacular leaps above the waves.

traits.title: Speed-Built Body
traits.description: Its smooth, pointed body slips through water at top speed.

traits.title: Crescent Tail
traits.description: Its stiff moon-shaped tail pushes it forward with strong beats.

mission.title: Mako Speed Chase

earlyReader: The tuna are very fast.
Count the tuna in each group.
Read the words to help the mako.
story: Race through open water with the fastest shark in the sea.
Count each group of tuna and read the words to help the mako catch up.

mission.completion: Whoosh! The mako used its speed to catch fast fish.

earlyReader: What is the mako best at?
story: Which skill makes the shortfin mako famous?

questions.success: Yes! The mako is the fastest shark.
questions.retry: Think about how it catches speedy fish.

earlyReader: What does the mako chase?
story: Which prey does a mako race after?

questions.success: Right! Makos chase fast fish like tuna.
questions.retry: Look for the food that swims.

earlyReader: Where does the mako live?
story: Which habitat belongs to a shortfin mako?

questions.success: You got it! Makos roam the open ocean.
questions.retry: Choose the wide blue water.

sharks.bookFact: It is the fastest shark and can leap high above the waves.

sharks.name: Basking Shark

decodable: It is big. It has a big, big gap.
earlyReader: This is a basking shark.
It is the second biggest fish.
It swims with its mouth wide open.
story: The basking shark is the second largest fish in the sea.
It cruises slowly with its enormous mouth open to gather tiny food.

decodable: It is not hot. It sits at the top in the sun.
earlyReader: Basking sharks like cool seas.
They often swim near the top.
They look like they bask in the sun.
story: Basking sharks live in cool and temperate seas around the world.
They often feed slowly at the surface, which looks like basking in the sunshine.

decodable: It has a gap. Bits bob in. It is fed.
earlyReader: Basking sharks eat plankton.
Plankton is very tiny food.
The shark just swims and swallows.
story: Basking sharks feed on tiny drifting animals called zooplankton.
They do not chase prey but simply swim forward with open mouths.

decodable: A bus is big. It is as big as the bus!
earlyReader: A basking shark is as long as a bus.
Its mouth opens as wide as a doorway.
Only the whale shark is bigger.
story: A basking shark can grow longer than twenty-six feet.
Its mouth can open more than three feet wide.

decodable: Bits bob at the top. It can get to the bits.
earlyReader: Plankton gathers in patches.
The shark finds the thick patches.
Then it swims back and forth to feed.
story: Basking sharks seek out places where plankton is most crowded.
They often follow lines in the sea where two kinds of water meet and food collects.

decodable: It has a net in his gap. The net gets bits.
earlyReader: Its gills have tiny combs.
The combs are called gill rakers.
They catch plankton as water flows out.
story: Long bristles called gill rakers line the basking shark's huge gill slits.
They strain plankton from the water like a giant comb.

traits.title: Gill Raker Comb
traits.description: Bristly gill rakers comb tiny plankton out of the water.

traits.title: Giant Gill Slits
traits.description: Its gill slits are so long they almost circle its head.

mission.title: Sunny Plankton Cruise

earlyReader: Plankton floats near the top.
Count the plankton you see.
Read the words to help the big shark.
story: Glide along the sunny surface with the basking shark.
Count each group of plankton and read the words as it swims with its mouth open.

mission.completion: Gulp! The basking shark filtered plankton with its gill rakers.

earlyReader: What does the basking shark eat?
story: Which food does a basking shark strain from the sea?

questions.success: Yes! Basking sharks eat tiny plankton.
questions.retry: Look for the tiny sparkling food.

earlyReader: How does it catch its food?
story: Which body part gathers a basking shark's meal?

questions.success: Right! It swims with its mouth wide open.
questions.retry: Think about what it opens very wide.

earlyReader: Where does it like to feed?
story: Where do basking sharks often feed?

questions.success: You got it! It feeds near the sunny surface.
questions.retry: Choose the place with water and sunshine.

sharks.bookFact: It is the second biggest fish and eats some of the smallest food.

sharks.name: Zebra Shark

decodable: The pup is not tan. The mom is tan and has dots.
earlyReader: This is a zebra shark.
Pups have stripes like a zebra.
Grown-ups have spots instead.
story: Zebra shark pups hatch dark with pale stripes, just like a zebra.
As they grow, the stripes break up into the dark spots of an adult.

decodable: It is hot. It sits on the mud and naps.
earlyReader: Zebra sharks live near coral reefs.
They rest on the sandy bottom.
The water is warm and shallow.
story: Zebra sharks live around coral reefs and sandy flats in the warm Indian and Pacific Oceans.
By day they often rest quietly on the seafloor.

decodable: It gets a bug and a bit in the mud. It sips it up.
earlyReader: Zebra sharks eat sea snails.
Clams and crabs are food too.
Strong jaws crush hard shells.
story: Sea snails, clams, crabs, and small fish are zebra shark food.
Its small mouth and strong jaws suck up and crush shelled prey.

decodable: It is big. It has a fin as big as him.
earlyReader: A zebra shark has a very long tail.
The tail is almost as long as its body.
Ridges run along its back.
story: A zebra shark can reach about eight feet long.
Nearly half of that length is its low, ribbon-like tail.

decodable: It is dim. Tap, tap. It can get a bit in the mud.
earlyReader: Zebra sharks hunt at night.
Small feelers sit near the mouth.
The feelers help find hidden food.
story: Zebra sharks are nocturnal and search for food after dark.
Short barbels on the snout help them feel for prey hidden in sand and coral.

decodable: It can fit in a gap. It can dig in and tug.
earlyReader: A zebra shark has a bendy body.
It wriggles into narrow cracks.
Hiding snails cannot get away.
story: A slender, flexible body lets the zebra shark squirm into narrow reef crevices.
There it reaches snails and crabs that other hunters cannot.

traits.title: Stripes to Spots
traits.description: Pups wear zebra stripes that change into spots as they grow.

traits.title: Ribbon Tail
traits.description: Its long, low tail is almost as long as the rest of its body.

mission.title: Night Snail Hunt

earlyReader: It is night on the reef.
Count the sea snails you see.
Read the words to help the shark.
story: Search the reef after dark with the zebra shark.
Count each group of sea snails and read the words to find them in the coral.

mission.completion: Crunch! The zebra shark found snails hiding in the reef.

earlyReader: What do zebra shark pups have?
story: Which pattern covers a zebra shark pup?

questions.success: Yes! Pups have stripes like a zebra.
questions.retry: Think about what a zebra wears.

earlyReader: What do grown-up zebra sharks have?
story: Which pattern replaces the stripes on an adult?

questions.success: Right! The stripes change into spots.
questions.retry: Look for the little round dots.

earlyReader: When does the zebra shark hunt?
story: When do zebra sharks search for food?

questions.success: You got it! Zebra sharks hunt at night.
questions.retry: Choose the dark, sleepy time.

sharks.bookFact: Its pups hatch with zebra stripes that turn into spots.

sharks.name: Blacktip Reef Shark

decodable: It has a dab on the tip of his fin.
earlyReader: This is a blacktip reef shark.
Each fin has a black tip.
It swims in very shallow water.
story: The blacktip reef shark wears a bold black tip on every fin.
It patrols warm, shallow water over coral reefs.

decodable: It is hot. The fin is up in the sun.
earlyReader: Blacktip reef sharks live on coral reefs.
The water can be only knee deep.
Sometimes a fin pokes above the water.
story: Blacktip reef sharks live on shallow coral reefs in the Indian and Pacific Oceans.
They swim in water so shallow that their back fins often show above the surface.

decodable: A mob of cod runs. It got a cod!
earlyReader: Blacktip reef sharks eat reef fish.
Squid and shrimp are food too.
They hunt along the edge of the reef.
story: Small reef fish make up most of a blacktip reef shark's meals.
It also eats squid, octopus, and shrimp.

decodable: It is not as big as a bus. It is as big as a mom.
earlyReader: This shark is about as long as a grown-up is tall.
It is small for a reef hunter.
Its body is slim and quick.
story: A blacktip reef shark usually grows to about five feet long.
Its slim body turns easily between coral heads.

decodable: A cod hid in a gap. It can get the hum.
earlyReader: Fish hide in the coral.
The shark smells and feels them.
It senses splashes in the water.
story: A blacktip reef shark uses smell and vibration to find fish among the coral.
Sensors along its sides feel the movement of prey nearby.

decodable: It runs at a mob of cod. The cod run to the rim.
earlyReader: Blacktip reef sharks can hunt as a team.
They push a school of fish to the shore.
Then the fish have nowhere to go.
story: Groups of blacktip reef sharks sometimes work together to herd schools of fish.
They drive the school into the shallows, where it is easier to catch.

traits.title: Black Fin Tips
traits.description: Every fin has a bold black tip, with a white band on the tall back fin.

traits.title: Shallow Swimmer
traits.description: It hunts in water so shallow that its fin sticks out.

mission.title: Reef Patrol

earlyReader: The reef is full of fish.
Count the reef fish you see.
Read the words to help the shark.
story: Patrol the shallow coral reef with the blacktip reef shark.
Count each group of reef fish and read the words as they dart from the coral.

mission.completion: Splash! The blacktip reef shark found fish in the shallow reef.

earlyReader: What is on the tips of its fins?
story: Which marking gives the blacktip reef shark its name?

questions.success: Yes! Every fin has a black tip.
questions.retry: Listen to the shark's name for a clue.

earlyReader: Where does this shark live?
story: Which habitat belongs to a blacktip reef shark?

questions.success: Right! It lives on shallow coral reefs.
questions.retry: Choose the warm place with coral.

earlyReader: What does it eat?
story: Which food does a blacktip reef shark hunt most?

questions.success: You got it! It eats small reef fish.
questions.retry: Look for the food that swims.

sharks.bookFact: Its black-tipped fin often pokes out of very shallow water.

sharks.name: Lemon Shark

decodable: It is tan. It sits on tan mud. It hid!
earlyReader: This is a lemon shark.
Its skin is yellow-brown.
It blends in with the sand.
story: The lemon shark is named for its yellow-brown skin.
That color helps it blend in over sandy seafloors near the coast.

decodable: The pup has a den. It hid in a gap in the den.
earlyReader: Lemon sharks live near warm coasts.
Pups grow up among mangrove roots.
The roots keep them safe.
story: Lemon sharks live in warm, shallow coastal water, bays, and river mouths.
Their pups spend their first years in mangrove nurseries, hidden among tangled roots.

decodable: It gets a cod. It gets a bug in the mud.
earlyReader: Lemon sharks eat fish.
Crabs and shrimp are food too.
Pups catch small food near the roots.
story: Lemon sharks eat mostly fish, along with crabs, shrimp, and rays.
Young sharks hunt small prey in the shallows of their nursery.

decodable: It is big. It has a fin and a fin on top.
earlyReader: A grown lemon shark is long and sturdy.
It has two back fins.
The two fins are almost the same size.
story: An adult lemon shark can grow to about ten feet long.
Unlike most sharks, its two back fins are nearly equal in size.

decodable: It is dim in the mud. It can get a hum.
earlyReader: Coastal water can be cloudy.
Lemon sharks do not need to see well.
They sense tiny electric signals instead.
story: Lemon sharks often hunt in murky water where eyes are little help.
Electric sensors in the snout and a sharp sense of smell lead them to prey.

decodable: The pup has a bud. The pup and his bud run and dip.
earlyReader: Lemon sharks like company.
Pups swim in friendly groups.
They can learn by watching each other.
story: Lemon sharks are unusually social and often gather in groups.
Scientists have found that young lemon sharks can learn new tasks by watching other sharks.

traits.title: Sandy Yellow Skin
traits.description: Its yellow-brown skin matches the sand below.

traits.title: Mangrove Nursery
traits.description: Pups grow up safely among tangled mangrove roots.

mission.title: Mangrove Hide-and-Seek

earlyReader: Lemon shark pups hide in the roots.
Count the mangrove roots you see.
Read the words to find a safe spot.
story: Help the lemon shark pups stay safe in their mangrove nursery.
Count each group of roots and read the words to find a hiding place.

mission.completion: Safe! The lemon shark pups hid among the mangrove roots.

earlyReader: Where do lemon shark pups grow up?
story: Which place is a nursery for lemon shark pups?

questions.success: Yes! Pups grow up among mangrove roots.
questions.retry: Look for the roots that stand in the water.

earlyReader: What helps it hide on the sand?
story: Which feature camouflages a lemon shark over sand?

questions.success: Right! Its yellow-brown skin matches the sand.
questions.retry: Think about the color of a lemon.

earlyReader: What helps it hunt in cloudy water?
story: Which sense works when the water is murky?

questions.success: Exactly! Electric sensors find hidden prey.
questions.retry: Choose the electric sparkle.

sharks.bookFact: Its pups grow up in mangrove nurseries with their friends.

sharks.name: Bull Shark

decodable: It is big. It can run up in the mud.
earlyReader: This is a bull shark.
It swims in the sea and in rivers.
Not many sharks can do that.
story: The sturdy bull shark swims along warm coasts and far up rivers.
Unlike most sharks, it can live in both salt water and fresh water.

decodable: It runs in the sun. It runs up to a dam.
earlyReader: Bull sharks like warm, shallow water.
They swim where rivers meet the sea.
Some swim far up a river.
story: Bull sharks live along warm coasts, in estuaries, and in rivers and lakes.
Some have been found hundreds of miles from the ocean.

decodable: It gets a cod. It gets a big bit.
earlyReader: Bull sharks eat many kinds of fish.
They eat stingrays too.
They hunt in cloudy water.
story: Bull sharks eat bony fish, stingrays, and other small sharks.
They often hunt in shallow, cloudy water near the bottom.

decodable: It is big and fat. It is not a pup.
earlyReader: A bull shark has a thick body.
Its snout is short and round.
It can grow longer than a rowboat.
story: The bull shark has a stout body and a short, blunt snout.
Large females can grow about eleven feet long.

decodable: The mud is dim. It can get a hum in the mud.
earlyReader: River water can be muddy.
A bull shark smells food from far away.
It feels fish moving in the water.
story: In muddy water a bull shark relies on smell, vibration, and electric senses more than sight.
These senses lead it to prey it cannot see.

decodable: Up, up, up it runs. It is fit in the mud.
earlyReader: Sea water is salty.
River water is fresh.
A bull shark’s body can handle both.
story: A bull shark’s kidneys and other organs adjust the salt and water inside its body.
That lets it move between the salty ocean and freshwater rivers.

traits.title: River Traveler
traits.description: It can swim from the salty sea into freshwater rivers.

traits.title: Sturdy Body
traits.description: Its thick body and blunt snout give the bull shark its name.

mission.title: River Journey

earlyReader: The river meets the sea here.
Count the river waves you see.
Read the words to help the shark swim on.
story: Guide the bull shark from the salty sea into a freshwater river.
Count each group of waves and read the words as it swims upstream.

mission.completion: Splash! The bull shark swam from the sea into the river.

earlyReader: Where can a bull shark swim?
story: Which place can a bull shark visit that most sharks cannot?

questions.success: Yes! It can swim up a river.
questions.retry: Choose the water that flows to the sea.

earlyReader: What does a bull shark eat?
story: Which food does a bull shark hunt?

questions.success: Right! Bull sharks eat fish.
questions.retry: Pick the food that swims.

earlyReader: What helps it find food in muddy water?
story: Which sense works well when the water is cloudy?

questions.success: Exactly! It can smell food in muddy water.
questions.retry: Choose the nose.

sharks.bookFact: It can swim from the salty sea far up freshwater rivers.

sharks.name: Longnose Sawshark
sharks.imageAuthor: ume-y (photo shows a Japanese sawshark, a close relative)

decodable: It has a big rod. The rod has tips.
earlyReader: This is a longnose sawshark.
Its snout looks like a saw.
Two long feelers hang from the snout.
story: The longnose sawshark carries a long, flat snout edged with sharp teeth.
It glides over sandy seafloors off southern Australia.

decodable: It is dim. It sits in the mud.
earlyReader: Sawsharks live near southern Australia.
They swim close to the sandy bottom.
The water there is cool.
story: Longnose sawsharks live over sand and gravel off the southern coast of Australia.
They stay near the seafloor, from shallow bays to deep water.

decodable: A bug hid in the mud. It can get the bug.
earlyReader: Sawsharks eat small fish.
They eat shrimp and squid too.
Their food hides in the sand.
story: Small fish, shrimp, and squid are a sawshark’s main foods.
Much of its prey hides in or just above the sand.

decodable: It is not big. It is as big as a kid.
earlyReader: A sawshark is long and thin.
It is about as long as a child is tall.
Its saw is a big part of its body.
story: A longnose sawshark grows to about four and a half feet long.
Its saw-shaped snout makes up more than a quarter of that length.

decodable: It can tap the mud. Is it a bug? It is!
earlyReader: Two feelers hang from the saw.
They are called barbels.
They touch the sand to find food.
story: Two long barbels trail from the middle of the sawshark’s snout and brush the seafloor.
Along with electric sensors in the snout, they help it find buried prey.

decodable: It can bat and hit. Rap, rap! It got a cod.
earlyReader: The saw has teeth on both sides.
The shark swings it from side to side.
The saw knocks small fish still.
story: A sawshark sweeps its toothed snout quickly from side to side.
The strike stuns small fish and stirs hidden prey out of the sand.

traits.title: Saw Snout
traits.description: Its long, flat snout has sharp teeth along both edges.

traits.title: Snout Feelers
traits.description: Two long barbels on its snout feel for food in the sand.

mission.title: Sandy Saw Sweep

earlyReader: Shrimp hide in the sand.
Count the shrimp you see.
Read the words to help the sawshark.
story: Glide the sawshark’s long snout just above the sandy seafloor.
Count each group of shrimp and read the words to sweep the saw.

mission.completion: Swish! The sawshark swept its saw and found its food.

earlyReader: What does a sawshark’s snout look like?
story: Which tool does a sawshark’s snout resemble?

questions.success: Yes! Its snout looks like a saw.
questions.retry: Look for the tool with teeth.

earlyReader: Where does a sawshark look for food?
story: Where does a sawshark search for prey?

questions.success: Right! It hunts along the seafloor.
questions.retry: Choose the sandy bottom of the sea.

earlyReader: What feels for food in the sand?
story: Which body part touches the sand to find prey?

questions.success: Exactly! Its barbels feel the sand.
questions.retry: Choose the soft feelers.

sharks.bookFact: Its long snout is a saw with teeth on both sides.

sharks.name: Cookiecutter Shark

decodable: It is not big. It can get a bit.
earlyReader: This is a cookiecutter shark.
It is a small shark from the deep sea.
Its belly glows green.
story: The small cookiecutter shark spends its days deep in warm oceans.
Its belly glows with a soft green light.

decodable: The sun set. Up it runs to the top.
earlyReader: Cookiecutter sharks live in warm oceans.
By day they stay very deep.
At night they swim up.
story: Cookiecutter sharks live in warm oceans around the world.
They spend the day in deep, dark water and rise toward the surface at night.

decodable: It gets a bit of a big cod. Nip!
earlyReader: This shark eats squid.
It also takes a small round bite from big fish.
The big fish swims away.
story: Cookiecutter sharks eat squid and take small round bites from much larger fish and whales.
The larger animal swims on, left with a round mark.

decodable: It is as big as a cat. It is not fat.
earlyReader: A cookiecutter shark is small.
It is about as long as a cat.
Its body is shaped like a cigar.
story: A cookiecutter shark grows to only about twenty inches long.
Its slim, rounded body once earned it the name cigar shark.

decodable: It is dim, but it can get a cod.
earlyReader: The deep sea is dark.
This shark has big eyes.
Big eyes catch a little light.
story: Large eyes help a cookiecutter shark gather the faint light of deep water.
Good vision helps it notice animals swimming nearby.

decodable: It is dim in the pit. But the gut is not dim!
earlyReader: Its belly makes green light.
A dark band crosses its throat.
The glow helps it hide from below.
story: Tiny light organs make the cookiecutter shark’s belly glow green.
From below, the glow blends with light from above, while a dark collar stays unlit.

traits.title: Glowing Belly
traits.description: Tiny lights make its belly glow green in the dark sea.

traits.title: Cookie Bite
traits.description: Its round mouth takes a small, cookie-shaped bite.

mission.title: Glow in the Deep

earlyReader: The deep water is dark.
Count the green glows you see.
Read the words to help the shark.
story: Dive into dark water where the cookiecutter shark’s belly shines green.
Count each group of glows and read the words before they fade into the deep.

mission.completion: Glow! The cookiecutter shark lit up the deep sea.

earlyReader: Where does it stay in the day?
story: Where does a cookiecutter shark spend the daytime?

questions.success: Yes! It stays in the deep ocean by day.
questions.retry: Choose the darkest underwater place.

earlyReader: What does its belly do?
story: What is special about a cookiecutter shark’s belly?

questions.success: Right! Its belly glows green.
questions.retry: Look for the green light.

earlyReader: When does it swim up?
story: When does a cookiecutter shark rise toward the surface?

questions.success: Exactly! It swims up at night.
questions.retry: Choose the time when the sky is dark.

sharks.bookFact: Its belly glows green in the dark, deep sea.

sharks.name: Angel Shark
sharks.imageAuthor: Julien Renoult (photo shows a common angelshark, a close relative)

decodable: It is a mat in the mud.
earlyReader: This is an angel shark.
Its body is flat and wide.
It hides under the sand.
story: The flat, wide Pacific angel shark looks more like a ray than a shark.
It lies hidden under sand on the seafloor.

decodable: It sits in the mud. The mud is on top of it.
earlyReader: Angel sharks live on sandy seafloors.
They rest near rocks and kelp.
Sand covers their backs.
story: Pacific angel sharks live on sandy and muddy bottoms along the eastern Pacific coast.
They often settle near rocky reefs and kelp forests.

decodable: A cod runs in. Up it pops! It got the cod.
earlyReader: Angel sharks eat fish.
They eat squid too.
The food swims right over them.
story: Pacific angel sharks eat bottom fish such as halibut and croakers, along with squid.
They catch prey that swims just above their hiding place.

decodable: It is as big as a kid. It is a fat mat.
earlyReader: An angel shark is flat like a pancake.
Its side fins are wide like wings.
It is about as long as a child is tall.
story: A Pacific angel shark grows to about five feet long.
Its broad pectoral fins spread out like wings beside its flat body.

decodable: It hid, but it is up. It can get a hum and a tap.
earlyReader: Its eyes sit on top of its head.
They peek out of the sand.
The shark watches for fish above.
story: An angel shark’s eyes sit on top of its head, so they stay clear when the body is buried.
It watches for the shape of prey passing overhead.

decodable: It hid and sat. Pop! It hit as a cod ran in.
earlyReader: The angel shark lies very still.
A fish swims close.
Snap! The shark lunges up fast.
story: A buried angel shark can wait in one spot for days.
When a fish swims close, it lunges upward and catches it in a fraction of a second.

traits.title: Sandy Disguise
traits.description: Its flat, speckled body disappears under the sand.

traits.title: Lightning Lunge
traits.description: It bursts up from the sand to catch a fish in a flash.

mission.title: Sandy Surprise

earlyReader: The angel shark hides under the sand.
Count the fish that swim close.
Read the words to help the shark.
story: Bury the angel shark in the sand and wait without moving.
Count each group of fish and read the words to pop out of the sand.

mission.completion: Whoosh! The angel shark popped out of the sand.

earlyReader: Where does an angel shark hide?
story: Where does an angel shark wait for prey?

questions.success: Yes! It hides under the sand.

sharks.name: Port Jackson Shark

decodable: It is tan. It has a rib on top.

They rest in caves and gullies by day and search for food at night.

story: Leopard sharks live in shallow bays and estuaries along the Pacific coast, from Oregon to Mexico.

story: Most grown leopard sharks are four to five feet long.

story: A leopard shark swims quietly just above the sand, looking for the tip of a clam poking out.

earlyReader: Leopard sharks swim in big groups.

story: Leopard sharks are strong swimmers that often gather in large schools.

sharks.name: Sand Tiger Shark

story: The sand tiger's long, pointed teeth show even when its mouth is closed.
It may look fierce, but it is a slow-moving shark with a calm nature.

earlyReader: Sand tigers live near shore.

story: Sand tigers live near the coast, around reefs, shallow bays and waves breaking on the shore.
They are often found around old shipwrecks.

earlyReader: Sand tigers eat fish.

story: A sand tiger eats many kinds of bony fish, such as herring, eels and sea bass.

earlyReader: A sand tiger is a big shark.

story: Sand tiger sharks are usually four to nine feet long.

story: Sand tigers hunt fish near reefs, surf and shallow bays.

story: A sand tiger swims to the surface and gulps air, which it holds in its stomach.

It lives so deep in the sea that people rarely see it.

earlyReader: Frilled sharks live very deep.

story: Frilled sharks live in deep water, usually near the seafloor on the slopes at the edges of the land.
They have been found thousands of feet below the surface.

story: Squid is the main food of the frilled shark, along with fish and other small sharks.

earlyReader: A frilled shark is long and slim.

story: Frilled sharks grow to about six and a half feet long.
Their slender bodies make them look more like eels than sharks.

story: Because frilled sharks live so deep, no one has watched them hunt in the wild.

story: The frilled shark has six pairs of gill slits, while most sharks have only five.

It swims slowly with its huge mouth wide open, straining food from the water.

earlyReader: A megamouth is very big.

story: Megamouth sharks grow to at least seventeen feet long.

story: Swarms of krill move up and down in the ocean each day.

earlyReader: The megamouth is a mystery.

It was so different from every other shark that scientists gave it a brand-new family.

During the day they tuck themselves into caves and cracks in the rocks.

story: A dwarf lanternshark has large eyes for its small, flat head.

sharks.name: Oceanic Whitetip Shark

story: Oceanic whitetips eat fish of the open sea, such as tuna and mackerel.

A few very large ones reach eleven feet or more.

story: Food is spread far apart in the open ocean.

sharks.name: Pyjama Shark

earlyReader: This is a pyjama shark.

story: The pyjama shark wears bold dark stripes, like a pair of striped pyjamas.
It is a small catshark that lives along the coast of South Africa.

earlyReader: Pyjama sharks live in South Africa.

story: Pyjama sharks live only along the coast of South Africa, on rocky reefs and in kelp beds.
They usually spend the day resting in caves and cracks.

Squid are a treat.
story: Pyjama sharks eat mostly crabs and other crustaceans, along with small fish.

story: A grown pyjama shark is usually two to three feet long.
A pup is about six inches long when it hatches.

story: A pyjama shark's eyes have a mirror-like layer that helps it see in dim light, much like a cat's eyes.

story: When it feels threatened, a pyjama shark curls into a ring like a donut.
It tucks its tail over its eyes and waits for a chance to slip away.

sharks.name: Bonnethead Shark

decodable: It has a fat top. It can tip it.
earlyReader: This is a bonnethead shark.

It is the smallest hammerhead.
story: The bonnethead is the smallest of the hammerhead sharks.
Its head is shaped like a rounded shovel, with an eye at each end.

decodable: It is in the sun. It is in a mob.
earlyReader: Bonnetheads like warm, shallow water.
They swim over sand, mud and seagrass.
They often swim in small groups.
story: Bonnetheads live in warm, shallow water over sand, mud, reefs and grass flats, and they are common in bays.
They usually swim in small schools of up to fifteen sharks.

decodable: It can nab a bug. It can nip a bud.
earlyReader: Bonnetheads eat crabs.
They eat shrimp and small fish too.
They even eat seagrass.
story: A bonnethead eats mostly crabs and shrimp, along with snails and small fish.
It also grazes on seagrass, which makes it a shark that eats both animals and plants.

earlyReader: A bonnethead is a small shark.

story: Most bonnetheads are three to four feet long, and the biggest reach about five feet.
Pups are about one foot long when they are born.

earlyReader: Its eyes sit at the ends of its head.

story: A bonnethead's eyes sit at the ends of its wide head, which lets it see more of the water around it.
As it swims, its head rolls from side to side.

decodable: It had a bud. It is fed. It is fit.
earlyReader: Most sharks eat only animals.
A bonnethead eats plants too.
An animal like that is called an omnivore.
story: Most sharks eat only other animals, but the bonnethead also grazes on seagrass.
An animal that eats both plants and animals is called an omnivore.

traits.description: It eats seagrass as well as crabs and shrimp.

sharks.name: Salmon Shark

decodable: It is big and fat. It can run.
earlyReader: This is a salmon shark.
It lives in cold water.
It is named for the salmon it eats.
story: The salmon shark is named for one of its favorite foods, the Pacific salmon.
This strong, heavy-bodied shark lives only in the North Pacific Ocean.

decodable: The sun is dim. It is not hot.
earlyReader: Salmon sharks live in the North Pacific.
The water there is cold.
They swim near Alaska and Japan.
story: Salmon sharks live in the cold and cool waters of the North Pacific, from Japan and Russia across to Alaska and California.
They swim both near the coast and far out at sea.

decodable: It ran at a cod. It got it.
earlyReader: Salmon sharks eat salmon.
They eat herring and cod too.
Squid can be food as well.
story: Salmon sharks eat many kinds of fish, including salmon, herring, pollock and cod.
They also eat squid.

decodable: It is big. Is a man as big? Not a bit!
earlyReader: A salmon shark is big and heavy.
Most are longer than a tall grown-up.
The biggest are about ten feet long.
story: Most salmon sharks are about six and a half to eight feet long.
The largest grow to about ten feet.

decodable: It is dim. It can get a hum.
earlyReader: Salmon swim in big groups.
Salmon sharks follow them.
The sharks go where the fish go.
story: Salmon sharks follow schools of Pacific salmon as the fish travel along the coasts.
Where there are plenty of salmon, there are often salmon sharks too.

decodable: It is dim, not hot. But his gut is hot.
earlyReader: Most fish are as cold as the water.
A salmon shark keeps its body warm.
Warm muscles help it swim fast in cold seas.
story: Most fish are the same temperature as the water around them, but a salmon shark can keep its body warmer than the sea.
Only a few fast swimmers, such as tunas and the salmon shark's close relatives, can do this.

traits.title: Warm Body
traits.description: It keeps its body warmer than the cold water around it.

traits.title: Salmon Follower

sharks.name: Porbeagle Shark

decodable: It has a fin. A dab is on it.
earlyReader: This is a porbeagle shark.
It has a white patch on its back fin.
It swims in cold seas.
story: The porbeagle is a strong, heavy-bodied shark of cold seas.
A white patch at the back of its tall dorsal fin helps people tell it from its relatives.

decodable: It is not hot. It is in the dim.
earlyReader: Porbeagles live in the North Atlantic.
They live in cold southern seas too.
They like cold water best.
story: In the north, porbeagles live only in the Atlantic Ocean, and in the south they circle the globe in a band of cold water.
They swim near coasts and far out at sea, from the surface to more than two thousand feet deep.

decodable: A mob of cod ran. It ran in.
earlyReader: Porbeagles eat fish.
Mackerel and herring are food.
Squid are food too.
story: Porbeagles eat mostly bony fish, such as mackerel, herring and cod.
Squid are their second most common food.

decodable: It is big and fit. It is not a pup.
earlyReader: A porbeagle is a big shark.
Its body is thick and strong.
The biggest are about twelve feet long.
story: Porbeagles have heavy, spindle-shaped bodies and can grow to about twelve feet long.
They may live for about thirty years.

decodable: It got a hum. It ran to it.
earlyReader: Fish move with the seasons.
Porbeagles move too.
They travel far to stay in cool water.
story: Like other big open-ocean sharks, porbeagles make long trips as the seasons change.
Scientists think these travels help them stay in the cool water they prefer.

decodable: It can run and run. It did not sit.
earlyReader: A porbeagle keeps its body warm.
Most fish cannot do that.
Tunas and a few other fast fish can.
story: A porbeagle can keep its body warmer than the cold water around it.
This is unusual among fishes, and only a few other fast swimmers, such as tunas, can do it.

traits.title: Warm Swimmer

sharks.name: Bluntnose Sixgill Shark

decodable: It is big. A fin is on top.
earlyReader: This is a sixgill shark.
It has six gill slits on each side.

story: The bluntnose sixgill shark has six long gill slits on each side of its head, while most sharks have five.
This big, slow, strong swimmer spends its days in deep water.

earlyReader: Sixgills rest in deep water by day.

story: By day a sixgill rests near the bottom in deep water, as far as six thousand five hundred feet down.
At night it swims up toward the surface or into shallower water to feed.

earlyReader: Sixgills eat at night.
They eat fish, big and small.
They eat crabs, shrimp and squid too.
story: A sixgill feeds at night on many kinds of animals, from cod and flounder to rays.
It also eats snails, crabs, shrimp and squid.

earlyReader: A sixgill is a very big shark.
It can be as long as a big car.
A new pup is as long as your arm.
story: The biggest sixgill sharks measured are almost sixteen feet long.
Pups are about two feet long when they are born.

decodable: The pit is dim. It got a hum.
earlyReader: A sixgill has big green eyes.
It lives where there is little light.
It hunts in the dark of night.
story: A living sixgill shark has large, glowing green eyes.
It spends its days in the dim deep sea and does its feeding at night.

decodable: It has ten pups. Ten and ten and ten!
earlyReader: A sixgill mother has many pups.
She can have more than twenty at once.
Some have had more than one hundred!
story: A mother sixgill gives birth to a very large litter of pups.
Scientists have counted from twenty-two to one hundred and eight pups in a single litter.

traits.description: It has six long gill slits on each side, one more than most sharks.

traits.description: It rests deep by day and swims up to feed at night.

sharks.name: Brownbanded Bamboo Shark

earlyReader: This is a bamboo shark.

As it grows up the bands fade, and adults are plain light brown.

earlyReader: Bamboo sharks live on coral reefs.
They live over sand and mud too.
Little ones hide in cracks.
story: Brownbanded bamboo sharks live on coral reefs and over sandy and muddy bottoms close to shore, from India to Japan and northern Australia.
Small ones hide in cracks in the reef, where their bands help them blend in.

earlyReader: Bamboo sharks eat at night.
They dig in the sand for food.
They eat crabs, worms and shrimp.
story: A bamboo shark is most active at night, when it digs in the sand and mud for food.
It eats crabs, worms, shrimp and small fish.

story: The biggest brownbanded bamboo sharks are about three and a half feet long.

earlyReader: Short feelers sit by its nose.

story: A bamboo shark has barbels, short feelers beside its nostrils, near the tip of its rounded snout.

story: The brownbanded bamboo shark is an extremely hardy shark that is often seen in tide pools.

earlyReader: Megalodon was a predator.

earlyReader: No one has found a whole megalodon.

story: The name megalodon means large tooth, and the biggest teeth are about seven inches long.

story: Scientists think megalodon's open jaws were about nine feet by eleven feet, and that its bite was far stronger than a great white shark's.

earlyReader: This is Mosasaurus.

story: Mosasaurs swam in warm seas all around the world, in the last part of the time of the dinosaurs.

story: Mosasaurs were top hunters that grabbed fish, squid and other sea animals.

story: The horn shark is named for the spine in front of each of its two back fins.

earlyReader: Horn sharks live by California.

story: Horn sharks live in shallow water from central California to Mexico, on rocky reefs and among kelp.

story: Unlike many sharks, a whitetip reef shark does not need to keep swimming to breathe.

sharks.name: Spiny Dogfish

earlyReader: Spiny dogfish live in cool seas.

story: Broadnose sevengill sharks live in cool seas and like shallow water close to shore, over rocks, sand and mud.
Mothers swim into shallow bays to have their pups, and the young sharks stay there for their first few years.

story: A broadnose sevengill shark can grow up to ten feet long.

story: Deep in the Gulf of Mexico, a tiny pocket shark swims through the dark.
Count each group of glows and read the words to light its way.

mission.completion: You did it! The tiny pocket shark glows in the deep, dark sea.

earlyReader: What does this shark have by each front fin?
story: What gives the pocket shark its name?

questions.success: Yes! It has a little pocket above each front fin.
questions.retry: Think about its name.

earlyReader: How big was the pocket shark?
story: How big was the pocket shark that scientists found?

choices.label: As big as a whale shark

questions.success: Right! It was shorter than a pencil.
questions.retry: It could fit in a pocket.

earlyReader: What do its pockets make?
story: What do the pocket shark's pockets make?

questions.success: You got it! The pockets make a liquid that glows.
questions.retry: Think about light in the dark sea.

sharks.bookFact: This tiny shark has a pocket by each front fin that makes a glowing liquid, and only two have ever been found.

earlyReader: Each whale shark has its own spot pattern.
Scientists take pictures of the spots.
The pictures help them recognize one shark again.
story: A whale shark's pale spots and stripes form a pattern that is unique to that individual.
Scientists use photographs of the pattern to recognize animals when they return to the same feeding place.

earlyReader: Trash can travel from land to the sea.
Plastic can hurt ocean animals.
We can use less plastic and put trash in the right bin.
story: Plastic and other marine debris can enter waterways and harm ocean animals.
Using reusable items and keeping litter out of drains helps protect feeding places for whale sharks and other sea life.

earlyReader: A hammerhead has a wide head.
Its eyes sit far apart at the ends.
The wide shape carries many electric sensors.
story: The hammer-shaped head is called a cephalofoil.
Its broad surface spreads the great hammerhead's eyes and electric sensors across a wide searching tool.

earlyReader: Sandy reefs are homes for many animals.
We can watch wild animals from a safe distance.
Clean water helps reef homes stay healthy.
story: Warm reefs and sandy coasts support many connected ocean animals.
Keeping waterways clean and giving wildlife space helps protect the places where hammerheads search for prey.

earlyReader: Nurse sharks have small feelers by their mouths.
The feelers are called barbels.
They help the shark search near the seafloor.
story: A nurse shark has two short barbels near its mouth.
These touch-sensitive feelers help it investigate cracks and sand while searching for hidden food.

earlyReader: Coral reefs need clean water.
Trash does not belong on a reef.
A clean home helps nurse sharks and their neighbors.
story: Nurse sharks rest and feed around reefs and seagrass beds.
Keeping litter out of the water helps protect the many small animals that share those coastal homes.

earlyReader: A great white has a pointed snout.
Its teeth are shaped for catching prey.
A strong tail pushes its big body through water.
story: Great white sharks have a streamlined body, a pointed snout, and a powerful tail.
Their triangular, serrated teeth help them hold and cut animal prey.

earlyReader: The open ocean is a busy animal home.
Wildlife needs clean water and space.
We can keep trash out of rivers and beaches.
story: Great whites travel through coastal and open-ocean habitats.
Keeping debris out of waterways and respecting wildlife from a distance supports healthier ocean places.

earlyReader: A wobbegong has little skin flaps by its mouth.
The flaps break up its outline.
They help the shark look like part of the seafloor.
story: Spotted wobbegongs have branching skin lobes around the mouth and a patterned body.
Together, these features help blur the shark's outline against rocks, sand, and reef.

earlyReader: The seafloor is a busy home.
Animals resting there need clean water.
We can leave wild places clean and quiet.
story: A wobbegong depends on a healthy seafloor for camouflage and hunting.
Keeping litter out of the ocean and observing wildlife without disturbance helps protect that habitat.

earlyReader: A thresher's top tail lobe is extra long.
It swings the tail like a whip.
The splash can stun small fish.
story: The thresher shark's upper tail lobe can be nearly as long as its body.
It uses that remarkable tail to strike close schools of fish and make prey easier to catch.

earlyReader: Open water is an animal home too.
Trash can drift a long way there.
Using less plastic helps keep water safer.
story: Ocean currents can carry marine debris far from where it first enters the water.
Reducing plastic waste helps protect open-ocean animals such as thresher sharks and their prey.

earlyReader: Young tiger sharks have dark stripes.
The stripes can fade as they grow.
Their broad heads help make a strong shape.
story: Young tiger sharks are marked with dark bars and spots that give the species its name.
The pattern often becomes less bold as the shark grows larger.

earlyReader: Coasts connect land and sea.
Trash on a street can reach the water.
Keeping drains clear helps ocean animals.
story: Storm drains and streams can carry litter from land toward coastal water.
Putting waste in the right bin helps protect the murky bays and reefs that tiger sharks visit.

earlyReader: An epaulette has sturdy paired fins.
It braces on the fins to move.
That helps it step across wet reef.
story: The epaulette shark uses its pectoral and pelvic fins in a walking motion.
This unusual movement helps it travel between shallow tide pools when water is low.

earlyReader: Tide pools are small ocean homes.
Tiny animals live between the rocks.
We can look gently and leave the pool clean.
story: Tide pools shelter many small animals when the tide falls.
Watching carefully, leaving animals where they are, and keeping litter away helps protect these shallow reef homes.

earlyReader: A goblin shark has a long flat snout.
Tiny electric sensors cover the snout.
Its jaws can shoot forward under the head.
story: The goblin shark's long flattened snout contains many electroreceptors.
When prey is close, its jaws can project forward in a dramatic slingshot motion.

earlyReader: The deep ocean is far away but still connected.
Trash can sink or drift through water.
Using less plastic helps every ocean zone.
story: Deep-sea habitats are connected to the rest of the ocean by moving water and sinking material.
Preventing debris before it reaches the sea is one way people can help protect animals far below the surface.

earlyReader: A Greenland shark has a thick body.
Small fins match its slow swim.
Cold water slows its body processes.
story: The Greenland shark has a heavy body and relatively small fins for its size.
Its cold-water life is linked to a very slow metabolism, movement, and growth rate.

earlyReader: Cold ocean water is an animal home.
Trash can travel to faraway coasts.
Using reusable things helps make less waste.
story: Ocean currents can move debris far from where people first drop it.
Choosing reusable items and disposing of waste properly helps protect cold-water habitats as well as warm ones.

earlyReader: A mako is shaped like a rocket.
Its back is deep blue and its belly is white.
Thin pointed teeth grip slippery fish.
story: The mako's metallic blue back and white belly help it disappear in open water.
Slender, pointed teeth hold on to fast, slippery prey.

earlyReader: Makos grow up slowly.
Too much fishing means fewer makos.
Fishing rules give them time to grow.
story: Shortfin makos grow slowly and have few pups, so their numbers recover slowly.
Careful fishing rules help mako populations rebuild.

earlyReader: A basking shark has huge gill slits.
They reach almost all the way around its head.
Water flows in the mouth and out the gills.
story: Five enormous gill slits nearly circle the basking shark's head.
Seawater streams through them while the gill rakers hold back food.

earlyReader: Basking sharks feed near the top.
Boats should slow down and give them room.
Watching from far away keeps them safe.
story: Because basking sharks feed at the surface, boats can disturb or bump them.
Slowing down and keeping a respectful distance lets them feed in peace.

earlyReader: A baby zebra shark is dark with pale stripes.
The stripes fade as it grows.
A grown-up is tan with dark spots.
story: Young zebra sharks are dark brown with pale yellow stripes.
Adults turn sandy tan with dark spots, so some people call them leopard sharks.

earlyReader: Zebra sharks need healthy reefs.
Coral can break when people touch it.
We can look at a reef and not touch.
story: Zebra sharks depend on healthy coral reefs for food and shelter.
Looking without touching and keeping the water clean help reefs stay alive.

earlyReader: Look at the tall fin on its back.
The tip is black with a white band below.
The other fins have black tips too.
story: A bright white band sits under the black tip of the blacktip reef shark's first back fin.
The bold markings make this shark easy to recognize in clear, shallow water.

earlyReader: Coral reefs are homes for many animals.
Reefs need clean, cool water.
Saving energy at home helps reefs far away.
story: Coral reefs shelter the fish that blacktip reef sharks eat.
Reefs stay healthiest in clean water that does not get too warm, so caring for the climate helps them.

earlyReader: A lemon shark has a yellow-brown back.
Its belly is pale.
It has a short, blunt snout.
story: A lemon shark's yellow-brown back fades to a pale belly.
Its head is broad and flat with a short, rounded snout.

earlyReader: Mangrove trees grow in salty water.
Their roots are a nursery for baby fish and sharks.
Keeping mangroves standing keeps pups safe.
story: Mangrove forests shelter young sharks, fish, and many other animals.
Protecting these trees along the coast protects the nurseries lemon sharks need.

earlyReader: A bull shark has a short, wide snout.
Its body is thick and strong.
That shape gave the bull shark its name.
story: The bull shark is named for its short, blunt snout and stocky body.
Its small eyes suit a life in cloudy water, where other senses matter more than sight.

earlyReader: Young bull sharks grow up where rivers meet the sea.
Clean rivers help the pups stay safe.
We can keep trash out of rivers and streams.
story: Estuaries, where rivers meet the sea, shelter young bull sharks while they grow.
Keeping rivers clean protects these nursery waters and the animals that depend on them.

earlyReader: A sawshark has gills on its sides.
A sawfish has gills under its body.
That is how you can tell them apart.
story: Sawsharks are true sharks, with gill slits on the sides of the head and barbels on the snout.
Sawfish look similar but are rays, with gills underneath and no barbels.

earlyReader: Sawsharks live near the seafloor.
Fishing nets can catch them by mistake.
Careful fishing helps seafloor animals.
story: Because sawsharks live near the bottom, they are sometimes caught by accident in fishing nets.
Careful fishing rules help keep seafloor animals and their habitats healthy.

earlyReader: A cookiecutter shark has a round mouth.
Its lips hold on like a suction cup.
Its bottom teeth are joined in a row.
story: Fleshy lips let the cookiecutter shark’s round mouth cling to a larger animal by suction.
Its lower teeth are joined together in a single row, like the edge of a saw.

earlyReader: The deep ocean is far from land.
Trash can still drift all the way there.
Using less plastic helps deep-sea animals.
story: Even the deep, open ocean is connected to land by moving water.
Keeping plastic out of waterways helps protect animals that live far below the surface.

earlyReader: An angel shark looks a bit like a ray.
But its gills are on its sides.
Its wide fins are not joined to its head.
story: Angel sharks have flat bodies like rays, but their gill slits are on the sides of the head.
Their wide pectoral fins are separate from the head, which shows they are true sharks.

earlyReader: Angel sharks rest on the seafloor.
Nets on the bottom can catch them by mistake.
Fishing rules help angel sharks stay safe.
story: Because angel sharks lie on the bottom, they are easily caught by accident in fishing nets.
Fishing rules that protect seafloor animals help Pacific angel sharks stay safe.

earlyReader: The mother lays dark spiral egg cases.
She wedges them between rocks.
A pup grows inside for many months.
story: A Port Jackson shark’s egg case is a dark spiral that the mother wedges into cracks in the rocks.
The pup inside takes close to a year to hatch.

earlyReader: Empty egg cases wash up on beaches.
You can look, but leave reef animals alone.
Clean reefs help shark eggs stay safe.
story: Each year Port Jackson sharks migrate back to the same reefs to lay their eggs.
Keeping those reefs clean and undisturbed helps the next generation hatch.

earlyReader: A blue shark has a slim body.
Its side fins are long and pointed.
Its snout is long like a cone.
story: A blue shark has a slender body, large eyes and a long, cone-shaped snout.
Its pointed side fins are very long, which helps tell it apart from other sharks.

earlyReader: Many blue sharks are caught in nets.
People catch more of them than any other shark.
Careful fishing helps keep them safe.
story: The blue shark is the most heavily fished shark in the world.
Scientists watch its numbers so that fishing rules can keep enough blue sharks in the sea.

earlyReader: A leopard shark is silver and gray.
Dark bars cross its back.
Old sharks have paler spots.
story: A leopard shark is silvery or bronze-gray on top and white underneath, with dark saddles across its back.
The older the shark, the paler the middle of each spot becomes.

earlyReader: Leopard sharks live a long time.
They grow up slowly.
Fishing rules help keep them safe.
story: Leopard sharks are not in danger now, but they grow slowly and could be hurt by too much fishing.
Fishing rules along the Pacific coast help protect them.

earlyReader: A sand tiger is light brown.
It has a few dark spots.
Its belly is pale.
story: A sand tiger is light brown on top with scattered dark spots, and pale underneath.
Its upper and lower jaws hold dozens of long, narrow teeth.

earlyReader: A sand tiger has only two pups.
Pups come every other year.
Rules keep people from catching them.
story: A mother sand tiger has just two pups every other year, so their numbers grow slowly.
Sand tigers have been fully protected along the Atlantic coast of the United States since 1997.

earlyReader: A frilled shark is dark brown.
Its mouth is at the very front.
It has only one back fin.
story: A frilled shark is dark brown or gray, with its mouth at the very front of its head instead of underneath.
It has just one fin on its back, while most sharks have two.

earlyReader: Frilled sharks live very deep.
Deep nets catch some by mistake.
Careful fishing helps them.
story: Frilled sharks are sometimes caught by accident in nets and lines set in deep water.
Careful fishing and protected ocean homes help keep these rare sharks safe.

earlyReader: A megamouth is gray on top.
It is pale underneath.
Its body and fins are soft.
story: A megamouth is gray to bluish-black on top and pale gray below.
Its soft, flabby body and floppy fins make it a slow swimmer.

earlyReader: Megamouths are very rare.
Scientists write down each one they see.
Each one teaches us something new.
story: So few megamouths have been seen that scientists keep a list of every confirmed sighting.
Each new sighting helps people learn how to protect this mysterious shark.

earlyReader: A swell shark is yellow-brown.
It has brown blotches and white spots.
Under blue light its skin glows green.
story: Brown blotches and white spots help a swell shark blend in with rocks and seaweed.
Scientists found that its skin glows bright green under the blue light of the sea.

earlyReader: Swell sharks can crawl into crab traps.
They can get stuck in nets too.
Careful fishing helps them stay safe.
story: People do not fish for swell sharks, but the sharks are sometimes caught by accident in traps and nets.
Careful fishing keeps more of these slow-growing sharks in the kelp forest.

earlyReader: This shark is dark brown.
It has a long, flat head.
Black marks run along its belly.
story: A dwarf lanternshark is dark brown with a long, flattened head.
A pattern of black markings on its underside helps scientists tell it from other lanternsharks.

earlyReader: This shark lives in one small part of the sea.
Deep nets can catch it by accident.
Scientists keep watch to keep it safe.
story: The dwarf lanternshark is known from only a small area and has just a few pups at a time.
It is not in danger today, but scientists watch that deep-sea fishing does not catch too many.

earlyReader: A spinner shark is gray on top.
Its belly is white.
Grown spinners have black tips on their fins.
story: A spinner shark is gray to bronze above and white below.
Adults have black tips on many fins, including the small fin under the tail.

earlyReader: Spinner pups are born near the shore.
Warm, shallow water is a safe start.
Clean coasts help the pups grow.
story: Spinner shark pups are born in shallow water close to shore during the summer.
Keeping coasts healthy protects the places where young sharks begin their lives.

earlyReader: This shark has a wide, strong body.
Its top fin is big and round.
Its side fins are long like paddles.
story: An oceanic whitetip has a stocky body, a big rounded fin on its back and very long, paddle-like side fins.
Its back is bronze-gray to brown, and its belly is white.

earlyReader: There used to be many whitetips.
Now there are far fewer.
Fishing rules help them come back.
story: Oceanic whitetips were once very common, but fishing has made them much rarer.
They are now protected as a threatened species, and fishing rules are helping in some places.

earlyReader: A pyjama shark is gray.
It has seven dark stripes.
Its belly is pale.
story: A pyjama shark is gray with seven broad dark stripes running along its back and sides.
Its two back fins sit far back on its body, close to the tail.

earlyReader: Pyjama sharks do not hurt people.
Some get caught on fishing lines.
Letting them go keeps the kelp forest healthy.
story: Pyjama sharks are harmless to people, but they are sometimes caught by people fishing for other animals.
Releasing them gently keeps these striped sharks in the kelp forest.

earlyReader: A bonnethead is gray or tan on top.
Its belly is pale.
Small dark spots may dot its sides.
story: A bonnethead is gray, tan or greenish on top with a paler belly, and its sides are often dotted with small dark spots.
Its rounded head makes it easy to tell from other hammerheads.

earlyReader: Bonnethead pups grow up in shallow bays.
Seagrass beds are their first home.
Healthy seagrass helps the pups grow.
story: Mother bonnetheads give birth in shallow water, and the young sharks live in seagrass beds for their first years.
Keeping bays and seagrass healthy protects the places where these small sharks grow up.

earlyReader: A salmon shark is dark on top.
Its belly is white with dark blotches.
Its snout is short and blunt.
story: A salmon shark is dark blue-gray to black on top and white underneath, and adults often have dusky blotches on the belly.
It has a heavy body, a short cone-shaped snout and a tail shaped like a crescent moon.

earlyReader: A salmon shark has only a few pups.
The pups take years to grow up.
Alaska has rules to keep them safe.
story: A mother salmon shark has only two to five pups at a time, so their numbers grow slowly.
Alaska closed commercial shark fishing in its state waters in 1997 and limits how many salmon sharks people may catch for sport.

earlyReader: A porbeagle is dark blue or gray on top.
Its belly is white.
Its snout is shaped like a cone.
story: A porbeagle is dark blue to gray above and white below, with a cone-shaped snout and a crescent-shaped tail.
The white tip at the back of its dorsal fin sets it apart from the salmon shark and the white shark.

earlyReader: There used to be many more porbeagles.
Too much fishing made them rare.
Fishing rules now help protect them.
story: Porbeagle numbers in the North Atlantic dropped badly because of too much fishing in the last century.
Today the porbeagle is protected in United States waters, and other countries limit how many may be caught.

earlyReader: A sixgill has a wide, flat head.
Its snout is round and blunt.
It has only one fin on its back.
story: A sixgill has a heavy body, a broad flat head and a blunt, rounded snout.
It has just one dorsal fin, set far back near its tail, and it is gray, olive green or brown with a paler belly.

earlyReader: Sixgills grow up very slowly.
Too much fishing can use them up.
Careful fishing helps them last.
story: Sixgill sharks take many years to grow up, so they cannot keep up with heavy fishing.
Scientists still need to learn how many there are, and careful fishing helps keep them in the deep sea.

earlyReader: A bamboo shark is long and slim.
Its tail is long and thick.
Its two back fins are about the same size.
story: A brownbanded bamboo shark has a slender body, a long thick tail and two dorsal fins of about the same size.
Its mouth sits close to its eyes, behind a rounded snout.

earlyReader: Bamboo sharks hatch from egg cases.
They need healthy coral reefs.
Careful fishing keeps reefs safe.
story: A mother bamboo shark lays flat egg cases on the bottom, and each pup grows inside for months before it hatches.
Harmful ways of fishing can damage the reefs where these sharks live, so protecting reefs protects them too.

earlyReader: A shark skeleton is made of cartilage.
Cartilage does not last like bone.
So we mostly find megalodon teeth.
story: Most of a shark's skeleton is cartilage, which does not turn into a fossil easily, so almost all megalodon fossils are teeth.
A few pieces of its backbone have been found too, each about the size of a dinner plate.

earlyReader: Megalodon teeth are found around the world.
Some are found in Florida.
Divers find them on the sea floor.
story: Megalodon teeth have been found on every continent except Antarctica.
Scientists measure the teeth, and compare them with sharks alive today, to work out how big megalodon was.

earlyReader: Most shark fossils are only teeth.
Cladoselache fossils show much more.
Some show skin and muscles.
story: It is very rare to find shark fossils that are not teeth, but the rock near Cleveland kept whole bodies of Cladoselache.
Some fossils even show traces of its skin, its muscles and the cartilage of its skeleton.

earlyReader: Fossil hunters look in creek banks.
They find hard lumps of stone.
A fossil can hide inside.
story: In nineteen twenty-seven, museum fossil hunters pulled a lump of stone up a creek bank and found the head and front fins of a Cladoselache inside.
Scientists are still studying these fossils, and some now think Cladoselache may be a closer cousin of ratfish than of the sharks alive today.

earlyReader: Sharks have no hard bones.
Their skeleton is cartilage.
Cartilage does not make good fossils.
story: Sharks are made of cartilage, which does not fossilize well, so much of what we know about the Ginsu shark comes from its teeth.
A few rare skeletons hardened enough to last, and they show how big it grew.

earlyReader: A fossil hunter found a Ginsu shark in Kansas.
It had a skull, teeth and a backbone.
A museum in Kansas keeps it safe.
story: In nineteen sixty-five, a collector named Sternberg dug a Ginsu shark skeleton out of the chalk in Ellis County, Kansas.
A university museum in Kansas keeps the skeleton, with its skull, its teeth and its backbone.

earlyReader: Helicoprion has cousins alive today.
They are called ratfish.
Its skeleton was made of cartilage.
story: Scientists place Helicoprion in a group of fish that includes the ratfish and chimaeras alive today.
Cartilage in its jaw held the tooth whorl firmly on both sides.

earlyReader: The tooth whorl was a puzzle.
For a hundred years, no one knew where it went.
A scan of a fossil showed the answer.
story: For about one hundred years, scientists had no idea where the coil of teeth sat on the body.
Then a team at a museum in Idaho scanned one of their best fossils, and the scan showed the spiral sitting in the lower jaw.

earlyReader: Its armor had a joint at the neck.
It could lift its head and drop its jaw.
That made a very wide mouth.
story: Dunkleosteus had joints between its head armor and its body armor, so it could lift its head while dropping its lower jaw.
Inside, its skeleton was cartilage, like a shark's, which is why only the armor is found.

earlyReader: Jay Terrell found the first fossils.
He found them by Lake Erie.
Now it is the state fossil fish of Ohio.
story: In eighteen sixty-seven, a fossil hunter named Jay Terrell found the first Dunkleosteus fossils in black rock on the shore of Lake Erie.
Many more were collected when a highway was built near Cleveland in the nineteen sixties, and the Cleveland Museum of Natural History keeps them today.

earlyReader: Mosasaurus had scales like a snake.
Its legs were paddles for swimming.
Snakes and monitor lizards are its relatives.
story: Mosasaurus was covered in scales like a snake, and mosasaurs had paddles for swimming where their land relatives have legs.
Mosasaurs did not have to come on land to have babies, because their young were likely born alive in the open sea.

earlyReader: Mosasaurus is extinct.
We know it from its fossils.
The first one was found in a rock quarry.
story: The first Mosasaurus fossil was found in the seventeen hundreds by miners digging in a limestone quarry near the city of Maastricht, in the Netherlands.
Its name means Meuse lizard, after the river that flows through that city.

earlyReader: An ichthyosaur had a smooth body.
It had a fin on its back.
Its tail was shaped like a crescent moon.
story: Later ichthyosaurs had smooth skin, a fin on the back and a tail shaped like a crescent moon.
Their bodies were shaped like those of tunas and dolphins, so scientists say they were built for speed.

earlyReader: Mary Anning lived by the sea in England.
Her brother Joseph found a strange skull.
Mary dug out the rest of the skeleton.
story: About two hundred years ago, when Mary Anning was twelve, her brother Joseph found a strange fossil skull near their home in Lyme Regis, England.
About a year later Mary dug out the rest of the skeleton, and the animal was named Ichthyosaurus, which means fish lizard, though it was neither a fish nor a lizard.

earlyReader: A plesiosaur had a short tail.
It had four flippers like paddles.
Elasmosaurus had the long-necked shape.
story: Plesiosaurs came in two shapes, long necked and short necked, and all of them had short tails and four flippers like paddles.
Scientists think their babies were very likely born alive in the open water.

earlyReader: An army doctor found the bones in Kansas.
A scientist put the head on the wrong end.
He thought the long neck was a tail!
story: A doctor named Theophilus Turner collected the bones of Elasmosaurus near Fort Wallace in Kansas, and they went by wagon and train to a scientist named Edward Cope.
At first Cope thought the long neck was the tail, so he put the skull on the wrong end.

earlyReader: Its shell was not one solid piece.
It was more like a frame of bones.
Its front flippers were big and flat.
story: The shell of Archelon was more like a frame of bones than one solid piece.
Its front flippers were large and flat, and scientists think it may have used its flippers and its big shell to protect itself.

earlyReader: Archelon is extinct.
Its bones were found in South Dakota.
The biggest skeleton is in a museum in Vienna.
story: The biggest Archelon skeleton was dug out of rock in South Dakota, where the shallow sea used to be, and it now stands in a museum in Vienna.
Archelon died out at the end of the time of the dinosaurs, along with about three out of every four kinds of living things.

earlyReader: Its tail pushed it through the water.
Its front legs were flippers.
It swam with a wave of its long body.
story: Scientists think Basilosaurus swam with a wave-like motion, using its tail to push and its front flippers to steer.
Its heavy ribs helped to keep it steady as it swam.

earlyReader: The first bone found was one backbone.
People thought it was a reptile.
Its teeth showed it was a mammal.
story: The first Basilosaurus fossil that scientists saw was a single bone from its back, and it was named king lizard.
Later a scientist named Richard Owen looked at its teeth, which each had two roots, and worked out that it was a mammal, and today it is the state fossil of Alabama.

earlyReader: A horn shark has a short, blunt head.
High ridges sit above its eyes.
It has small dark spots and two fin spines.
story: A horn shark has a short, blunt head with a high ridge above each eye, and a sharp spine in front of each back fin.
Its skin is gray or brown with small dark spots, which helps it stay hidden.

earlyReader: Horn sharks are doing well.
Some get caught in crab traps by mistake.
Good divers look and do not touch.
story: Horn sharks seem to be doing well, but some are caught by accident in crab traps and nets.
Where many divers have caught them for their spines, their numbers have gone down, so it is best to look and not touch.

earlyReader: This shark is long and slim.
Its head is wide and flat.
Its snout is short and blunt.
story: A whitetip reef shark has a slender body, a broad flat head and a very short, blunt snout.
Its eyes are oval, and its back fin and the top of its tail are tipped with white.

earlyReader: A mother has only a few pups.
So these sharks need time to grow in number.
Safe reefs help them.
story: Whitetip reef sharks have small families and grow up slowly, so their numbers take a long time to recover.
Protected reefs, where fishing is limited, may help keep them safe.

earlyReader: A spiny dogfish is gray on top.
It is white below.
Young ones have a row of white spots.
story: A spiny dogfish is slim and gray above and pale below, with a row of small white spots along each side that fade as it grows older.
The sharp spine in front of each back fin helps it defend itself.

earlyReader: Dogfish grow up slowly.
They can live 35 years or more.
Rules on fishing help keep enough of them in the sea.
story: Spiny dogfish grow slowly and can live for 35 to 40 years, and a mother carries her pups for up to two years before they are born.
Because of that, too much fishing can harm them, so there are limits on how many may be caught.

earlyReader: Most sharks have two back fins.
This shark has only one.
Its skin has many small dark spots.
story: A sevengill shark has only one back fin, set far back on its body, while most sharks have two.
Its back and sides are gray or brown and speckled with many small black spots.

earlyReader: Sevengill pups grow up in bays.
Long ago, too many were caught in one bay.
Healthy bays help pups grow.
story: Bays are important nurseries for sevengill pups.
Because these sharks stay close to shore they are easy to catch, and long ago too many were taken from San Francisco Bay.

earlyReader: A silky shark is long and slim.
It is dark gray on top.
Its belly is white.
story: A silky shark is dark gray with a bronze tint on top and white underneath.
Its front fins are long and slender, usually with dusky tips, and its second back fin is small with a long trailing tip.

earlyReader: Silky sharks grow slowly.
They have only a few pups.
Some get caught when people fish for tuna.
story: Silky sharks grow slowly and have only two to fourteen pups at a time, so too much fishing can harm them.
They are often caught by accident by boats fishing for tuna, so careful fishing helps keep them in the sea.

earlyReader: A shyshark is golden brown.
It has reddish-brown saddles.
It has small white spots.
story: A puffadder shyshark is golden brown with reddish-brown saddles edged in a darker color and dotted with small white spots.
Its markings look like those of a snake called the puff adder, and that is how it got its name.

earlyReader: Shysharks do not hurt people.
They are endangered.
Careful fishing helps keep them safe.
story: Puffadder shysharks are harmless to people, but they are endangered and live in only one small part of the world.
They get caught by accident in fishing gear, so careful fishing and healthy kelp forests help them.

earlyReader: A kitefin shark is dark brown.
Its snout is short and blunt.
Its fins have pale edges.
story: A kitefin shark is dark brown or grayish black all over, with a short, blunt snout and thick lips.
The edges of its fins are white or see-through, and the tip of its tail is black.

earlyReader: Kitefin sharks do not hurt people.
People fish for them for their oil.
Careful fishing helps them last.
story: Kitefin sharks are no danger to people because they live so deep.
They are caught for the oil in their livers, and scientists think they have young slowly, so careful fishing matters.

earlyReader: A pocket shark has a big round head.
It has rows of tiny teeth.
New teeth grow in behind the old ones.
story: A pocket shark has a rounded, bulb-shaped head and rows of tiny, sharp teeth.
Scans showed new teeth coming up to replace the ones that were missing.

earlyReader: This shark is very rare.
Scientists kept it whole.
They used a scanner to look inside.
story: Because the pocket shark is so rare, scientists looked inside it with a special scanner, so it could be kept whole.
They shared the pictures so that everyone can learn about this little shark.
